in_context.text: Paul is asking Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, who had left him and had since become a believer through Paul in prison. Here Paul gently suggests a reason behind that departure: Onesimus was away for a short time so that Philemon might have him back for good. The next verse says how: no longer only as a servant, but as a beloved brother.

speaker.text: Paul, who calls himself a prisoner of Jesus Christ, writing with Timothy.

audience.text: Philemon, Paul's beloved fellow-worker, along with Apphia, Archippus and the church that met in his house.

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant, whom Paul calls "my son" and is sending back.

what.text: Paul offers a hopeful way to see Onesimus's leaving. It may have been for a purpose: a brief separation that ends in a lasting bond. Paul says "perhaps," so he does not claim to know this for certain.

events.text: Onesimus had earlier "departed" from Philemon and had been "unprofitable" to him. Since then he had met Paul in prison and become a believer. Now Paul was sending him back.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 60-62, while Paul was imprisoned in Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly view: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul wrote from prison; the letter does not name the city, and Rome is the traditional view. It was sent to Philemon's house church, most likely in Colossae, since Colossians calls Onesimus "one of you."

purpose.text: Paul wants Philemon to receive Onesimus willingly, not by force. Pointing to a possible good purpose in the separation helps Philemon see the return as a gift rather than a loss.

big_picture.text: Scripture often shows God bringing good out of a painful parting. Joseph told his brothers, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." Paul hints at something similar here, but only with a "perhaps."

for_readers.text: Readers can look at past breaks in relationships with hope that God may use them for lasting good. They can also follow Paul's humility in not claiming to know God's purpose for sure.

why_it_matters.text: The lexicon glosses it "perhaps" and lists only one other New Testament use, Romans 5:7. Paul offers his reading of events as a possibility, not a certainty.
The word here is rendered "he was separated [from you]." The lexicon defines it as to separate, and lists this verse under the sense to separate oneself or depart.

The lexicon says the phrase means "for a season, for a time," as also in John 5:35, 2 Corinthians 7:8 and Galatians 2:5. In this verse it is set against "for ever," so the short absence is weighed against the lasting return.
The lexicon glosses it "eternal" and lists the sense "that which is without end." Verse 16 shows the lasting bond is that of "a brother beloved" in the Lord.
The lexicon defines it as to have in full, and for this verse gives "to have altogether." Philemon would get Onesimus back fully, not partly.

takeaway.text: Paul humbly suggests that a short, painful separation may have had a purpose: lasting brotherhood in Christ. He invites Philemon to look at the loss that way and welcome Onesimus as a brother.
